analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal job guarantee program at living wages, funded by a tax on stock and bond trades.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Frederica Wilson, drew zero cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a National Full Employment Trust Fund to pay for public service jobs — in childcare, housing repair, parks, schools, and community services — for anyone certified as unemployed or stuck in part-time work, paying wages comparable to local public-sector pay. The money would come from a new tax on securities trading: 0.2% on stock trades and 0.06% on bond and most derivative trades, with the Federal Reserve authorized to lend the fund more if unemployment rises. It is modeled on New Deal-era direct job creation and the 1978 Humphrey-Hawkins full employment law.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and involuntarily part-time workers who want full-time work would get access to a government-funded job at pay and benefits comparable to local public-sector employees, plus help with training, placement, and benefits enrollment. Projects would serve high-poverty areas and require at least 35% of hires to be disadvantaged workers.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a standing federal jobs program in which any eligible person can get a 35-40 hour per week job funded by the Trust Fund, with no displacement of existing workers allowed [S2].

Requires compensation comparable to similar local public-sector work, including health benefits obtained through ACA exchanges with premiums paid via employer payroll deductions, and prevailing wages on construction work [S2].
Grants prioritize projects in areas with high unemployment, poverty, concentrated poverty, and foreclosure rates, and require at least 35% of employees to be certified disadvantaged individuals [S2].

Grants must spend at least 75% of funds on wages, benefits, and support services like childcare, and grantees must provide job training and assisted placement for people who struggle to find work [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions and active traders would pay a new tax on securities transactions — 0.2% on stock sales and 0.06% on bonds and most derivatives — collected from exchanges and brokers, and the cost would partly be passed through to investors. The Federal Reserve would also be required to lend to the fund if unemployment rises more than one percentage point.

drawbacks.text: The trading tax would be collected on nearly all securities purchases, and while mutual fund shares are exempt, investors in stocks, ETFs, and bonds — including people trading through retirement accounts — would bear some of the cost through their brokers [S2].

The bill requires the Federal Reserve to lend the fund whatever is needed whenever unemployment rises more than one percentage point, a mandate that would remove monetary policy flexibility and draw the central bank directly into fiscal job creation [S2].

A permanent federal guarantee of a job for anyone unemployed is a very large open-ended spending commitment whose total cost is not estimated anywhere in the bill, and disputes over eligibility and discipline are routed to a new administrative office whose process would replace other legal remedies once chosen [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — a job at living wages for anyone who cannot find one — would directly help the people unemployment hurts most, and the bill includes real protections against displacing existing workers or subsidizing union-busting. But it is an enormous and largely uncosted commitment, its dedicated funding source is a trading tax that would touch ordinary investors as well as Wall Street, and its Fed-lending mandate would force the central bank into a role Congress has never assigned it. The design is ambitious and ideologically coherent, but the price tag and administrative burden are untested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, eventually sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson introduced the bill on April 5, 2024; it was referred the same day to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S4].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its entire life [S3].
On December 17, 2024, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare, the last action of its history [S4].
Neither committee took it up, no version ever reached the House floor, and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions and frequent traders who would have paid the new securities transaction tax are better off because the bill never advanced. Unemployed workers who would have qualified for program jobs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that avoided the trading tax

for.name: Rep. Frederica Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Jobs for All Act and was its only sponsor for the entire Congress.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction, referred it to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare in December 2024, and never held a markup or vote.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Secondary committee of referral (jurisdiction over the tax title)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never acted on it, including on its securities-trading tax provisions.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Presided over the primary committee of referral, which never considered the bill.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Presided over the committee with jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions, which never considered the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no partisan split is on the record; the single sponsor was a Democrat, not one of her 215 Democratic colleagues cosponsored, and the bill sat in Republican-controlled committees until the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill's entire funding source is a new tax of 0.2% on stock trades and 0.06% on bond and most derivative trades, collected from exchanges and brokers; derivatives, options, and futures payments are taxed as separate transactions. The industry's opposition to such a tax is the bill's main cost, and the money would fund jobs for ordinary people.

Tax-exempt nonprofits, local governments, tribes, and public agencies would be eligible for Employment Opportunity Grants funding staff for childcare, health services, housing repair, parks, and schools. Their gain runs alongside the public services their communities receive.

The bill funds extra public-sector staffing but bars program hires from replacing laid-off workers or filling positions local governments could fund themselves, protecting existing public employees while adding capacity for services.
